source: Curated starting assumptions for the watchlist
note: These are considered STARTING assumptions with written reasoning, not recommendations and not forecasts. They exist to be argued with: every value is editable and 'Reset overrides' returns to raw street consensus. Where they differ from consensus the reason is stated, because a model that silently disagrees with the street is worse than one that agrees.

house_view.terminal_growth: FMP defaults terminal growth to 4% (6% for MU). Nominal long-run GDP is nearer 4% and no company grows faster than the economy in perpetuity, so a terminal g at or above it capitalises an impossibility. These use 2.0-3.0%, scaled to franchise durability.
house_view.equity_risk_premium: 4.5% throughout, close to current implied ERP. FMP's 4.72% is defensible; this is marginally more conservative.
house_view.risk_free: Live 10-year Treasury from FMP's treasury-rates endpoint, currently ~4.78%.
house_view.cyclicals: Semiconductor and memory margins are normalised toward mid-cycle rather than extrapolated from the current point in the cycle. Discounting peak margins to perpetuity is the standard way to lose money in semis.
house_view.fade: Growth fades toward terminal over the forecast rather than stepping down at the terminal year. A DCF whose terminal year is also its peak year embeds a discontinuity.
house_view.read_it_this_way: Every name here prices above the model, so read the market-implied terminal growth rather than the downside percentage — a model that says the whole market is wrong is usually the thing that is wrong. Implied g at current prices: NEE 3.9%, COST 7.0%, APH 7.1%, NVDA 10.5%, AMD 13.7%, MU 14.1%, against 2.5-3.0% assumed here. Only NEE's is defensible as perpetuity growth. Above roughly 4% nominal GDP the price is not being set by a perpetuity DCF at all — it embeds a longer explicit forecast, cycle earnings, or option value that this five-year structure cannot represent. That is a statement about the tool's limits as much as about the price.
house_view.what_this_is_not: Not a recommendation, not a price target, and not a forecast. A five-year DCF with 64-85% of value in the terminal is mostly an opinion about the terminal, expressed with false precision. The useful output is the disagreement it exposes, not the per-share number.

NVDA.thesis: Extraordinary current economics; the whole valuation question is how fast the margin normalises.
flags: 60% operating margin is roughly double any historical semiconductor peak. Faded, not held flat.
rationale: Revenue grew 126%, 114%, 65% — decelerating hard even while enormous. Street has 89% then fading to 8%. Accepted broadly, because the order book is real, but the back half is trimmed: the base is now $216bn and compounding off that is arithmetically harder.

This is the assumption that matters. A 60% operating margin exists because supply is scarce and competition is absent. Both change: AMD is shipping, hyperscalers are building custom silicon, and memory is now the binding constraint. Faded 60% to 48% over five years — still exceptional, just not permanent.
Fabless, so capex stays ~3% of revenue. The capital intensity sits in the supply chain, not the balance sheet.
3.0%. Accelerated compute is a genuine secular shift, so a premium to GDP is defensible; a durable 60% margin is not, which is why the fade does the work rather than the terminal rate.
risks: Customer concentration — a handful of hyperscalers are most of revenue.
Margin mean-reversion is the single largest sensitivity.
Export controls on the China business.

AMD.thesis: Real share gain, but the street's margin step-up is a year early.
flags: Street models a 26.5% EBIT margin against 10.7% actual — a 16-point jump in one year. Phased over three.
rationale: 34% revenue growth and genuine MI-series traction. Street's 47% then 74% is plausible in direction and aggressive in slope; trimmed to 40% then fading, because AMD is supply-constrained by the same packaging and memory bottlenecks as everyone else.

Gross margin ~49.5% is credible and improving with mix. Operating margin is the disagreement: 10.7% today, street at 26.5% next year. Modelled 16% to 22% over five years — the operating leverage is real, but AMD carries heavier R&D intensity than NVIDIA and discounts to win sockets.
Fabless, capex ~3%. Balance sheet is nearly unlevered (D/E 0.07), so the WACC is almost entirely cost of equity — and with beta 2.48 that is punishing.
risks: Beta 2.48 makes the discount rate dominate the answer.
Competes with a rival earning 60% margins and funding R&D from it.

MU.thesis: Peak-cycle earnings. The street model capitalises the peak; this one does not.
flags: Street shows +246.6% revenue with a 74.7% EBIT margin against 26.4% actual. FMP's own DCF uses a 6% terminal growth rate. Both are rejected here — this is the largest deviation from consensus on the list, and deliberately so.
rationale: The cycle is the whole story

Operating margin by fiscal year: -37.0%, +5.2%, +26.4%. That is not a trend, it is a cycle. HBM demand is genuinely structural, but memory has repeatedly converted structural demand into oversupply. Modelling the upswing forward to perpetuity is the classic semis error.
Near-term strength accepted but heavily trimmed: 90% then fading to mid-single-digit. The street's 247% is a price-driven spike, and price spikes in memory mean-revert.

Normalised toward mid-cycle: 45% gross fading to 35%, operating settling near 22% rather than the 74% peak the street implies. Through-cycle, Micron earns a mid-20s operating margin in good years and loses money in bad ones.
Capex is 42% of revenue and D&A 22% — this business consumes cash to stand still. Held high deliberately; a memory model with light capex is not a memory model.
2.5%. A commodity manufacturer with periodic negative earnings does not deserve a growth premium.
risks: If the cycle runs hotter and longer, this model is badly too conservative — that is the honest failure mode.
Capital intensity means a downturn hits FCF immediately.
Beta 2.22 plus cyclicality gives a very high discount rate.

COST.thesis: One of the best businesses on the list, and the model will almost certainly say it is expensive. Both things are true.
rationale: Remarkably steady: 6.8%, 5.0%, 8.2%. Membership renewal rates and warehouse openings make this among the most predictable revenue lines in retail. Modelled 8% fading to 5.5%.

Gross margin is only 12.8% and operating 3.8% — and that is the point, not a weakness. Costco deliberately runs thin merchandise margins and earns its return on membership fees and turns. ROIC is 19% on those margins. Modelled with slow creep to 4.1%; assuming more would misunderstand the model.
Capex ~2% of revenue, low leverage, negative working capital — it is paid by customers before it pays suppliers. That funds growth internally.
2.5%. Durable franchise, but a retailer cannot outgrow nominal GDP forever.
At ~$916 and 40x+ earnings the DCF will likely show meaningful downside. That is the model working, not failing — quality and price are separate questions and this page only answers the second.
risks: Multiple compression is the dominant risk, not operations.
Membership fee increases are the main margin lever and they are infrequent.

APH.thesis: High-quality serial acquirer; the reported growth rate is not the organic growth rate.
flags: FY25 revenue grew 51.7% and street models +52.7% again. Much of that is acquisition, not organic. Modelled closer to underlying.
rationale: Growth by year: -0.5%, 21.3%, 51.7%. A company does not organically accelerate from -0.5% to 51.7%; that is M&A plus an AI-datacentre interconnect surge. Modelled 30% then fading to 8%, which credits the current cycle without assuming the acquisition cadence continues indefinitely.
Operating margin has expanded 20.7% to 25.9% and held. Amphenol's decentralised operating model genuinely does protect margins through integration. Held near 25.5%.
Capex ~4% of revenue. The real capital use is acquisitions, which the model does not project — so this understates both the cash outflow and the growth it buys. Worth knowing when reading the output.
risks: Roll-up economics depend on continued disciplined pricing on deals.
Datacentre interconnect demand is correlated with the same AI capex cycle as NVDA and AMD — less diversification than it appears.

NEE.thesis: Regulated utility with a renewables growth arm — a bond proxy with a capex problem.
flags: Street models a 45.4% EBIT margin against 30.1% actual. Utility margins are set by regulators and do not jump 15 points; held near reported.
rationale: Rate-base growth plus renewables development, roughly 7-8% and unusually visible because it is contracted and regulated. Street's 12.6% is at the optimistic end; modelled 8% fading to 6%.
Operating margin has been 36.4%, 30.2%, 30.1%. Regulated returns are allowed, not earned at will. Held ~30%, rejecting the street's 45%.

Capex is 34% of revenue and D&A 25% — this is the defining feature. NextEra outspends its operating cash flow and funds the gap with debt and equity issuance, which is why D/E is 1.75. FCF is structurally thin; the DCF will reflect that honestly.
Beta 0.64 gives a WACC near 7.6% — the lowest on the list. That is doing a lot of work in the valuation, and it is precisely the number that rises if rates do.
2.5%, consistent with regulated rate-base growth over the long run.
risks: Rate sensitivity cuts both ways: low WACC flatters the value, and a higher-for-longer curve reverses it directly.
Heavy capex plus 1.75 D/E means financing conditions matter as much as operations.
Renewables policy and tax-credit regime risk.
